items.author: ArshadAzeezM
items.content: Everything a cut needs, by hand or by asking. Captions are transcribed with word timing and styled with reusable presets. Silences and filler words come out of a talking head in one pass, and Tab suggests your next edit as you work. Colour has wheels, curves, HSL secondaries, LUTs and shot matching. Audio has voice isolation, noise reduction, loudness and automatic ducking under speech. Images, video, voiceover, music and sound effects are generated straight onto the timeline. Export an MP4 with no watermark, or hand off to DaVinci Resolve and Premiere Pro as FCPXML. Arsaze also has background removal, motion tracking, Animate Studio motion graphics, a node editor for AI generation, an After Effects panel (beta), a free portfolio page and free in-browser tools. Every tool works by hand on the timeline, and every one is also a tool your AI can call.

items.title: Show HN: I Turned DOOM into a Transformer
items.author: falperc
items.content:
Instead of trying to run DOOM on things, I have instead decided to use DOOM (many, many, many doom games actually) to create a transformer. For a lot of the math required I essentially had to use DOOM game mechanics and voodoo dolls (DOOM is turing complete btw) and exchange them with the actual operations, essentially creating an alternative to NumPy (a 65000x slower one). Thus, I am proud to present DOOMFORMER. Here are a list of things DOOMFORMER can do :

It can classify MNIST digits, even if you write these digits on the map!

You can use it to make decisions, so, it can play DOOM. Yes! You can play DOOM with thousands of DOOM games now! The marine's mind can be controlled by DOOM, playing on a map generated by DOOMFORMER. Truly, the possibilities are endless, and even larger-scale training of DOOMFORMER could be done on a measly T4.

If anyone would like to help me scale this up and make crazier things, I'd love to work together.

items.title: Show HN: A proof-of-concept formalization of the IRS federal tax forms
items.author: RGS1811
items.content:
The linked repo is 100% vibe coded, but it was built on a handful of principles:

- Most tax software derives trust from the party who maintains it (e.g. Intuit, the IRS, etc.)

- Vibe coded software lacks this trustworthiness.

- Therefore any formalization should build in verifiability and mechanisms that make it possible for users/maintainers to trace claims/interpretations back to authoritative source documents.

It's very much a back-burner passive project right now (do not use this for anything real!), but I feel strongly that something like this ought to exist for the public good. I built it to get a sense of what the shape of what such a thing might be.

items.title: Show HN: Hob - Open-source, on device alternative to Claude Cowork and ChatGPT
items.author: pancomplex
items.content:
Hey HN, I'm Christian and this is a new OSS project I've been noodling on for the last couple of weeks. Hob is a free, MIT-licensed desktop app for Mac, Windows and Linux that works on your files the way the Claude and ChatGPT desktop apps do, except the model runs on your own computer. It uses open-weight models (currently Gemma 4 and gpt-oss). All your chats and files never leave your system. The only things that go online are web search (can be turned off in settings) and any MCP connectors you add yourself.

- Automatically finds the best open-weight model for your hardware on first install (Mac/Linux/Windows)

- Writes sandboxed Python code for ad hoc tools (data processing, document conversion, graphs etc.)

- Built-in web search (powered by SearXNG)

- CRUD to your local filesystem

- Works fully offline with no internet

Before building this I tried every local AI app I could find, but it seemed each one had different problems. The main thing I noticed is that none of them could do what the ChatGPT and Claude apps do with your files, e.g. read and change files in a folder, look at images, run code in a sandbox, draw a chart. The most advanced thing any of them did was paste a plain text file into a small context window, which basically failed as soon as you had a file larger than a few KB. I couldn't find anything that could easily parse images and bigger PDFs.

The OSS solutions that were more advanced all seemed to default to hosted models (either OSS or closed), which defeats the entire point of the privacy that on-device OSS offers. They also seemed to push towards an account/open-core style business.

I build it using Electron bridged with llama.cpp in its own process. On initial load, the system will try and figure out if you have a compatible graphics card and if not default to CPU-only (I ran into a lot of issues of graphics card beeing seemingly compatible but then crashing on first query, there's a whole saga to this lol). Code execution happens in a sandbox that can only write to the chat's folder and has no network unless asked (sandbox-exec on macOS, Landlock on Linux and a low-integrity process on Windows). Images go to a small Qwen3-VL model. Dictation is a local Whisper model.

The hardest part was definitely to get the smaller models to use tools reliably. Ran into a ton of issues of 4B models happily saying "here's your chart" without ever calling the chart tool or get stuck in an infinite call loop. I spent a fair amount of the work building guards vs tweaking prompts (that didn't really work for small models).

I understand the pushback that local models are weaker than frontier cloud models. This is true, but for most tasks for most normal people, I'd argue you rarely need the newest frontier model. From my own evals, systems with 16+ GB of RAM do really well, and if you have a GPU or more RAM, you get very close to what you'll get out of the box with a frontier hosted model.

Excited to hear what you think and see how it runs on other systems!

items.title: Show HN: Hurston-1 open source TTS that speak Southern American and Afro-English
items.author: Gcarter08
items.content:
Accented English text-to-speech built for the phone, steered by a plain-language voice description.

Hurston-1 introduces : text-to-speech made for the phone line, where most customer service still happens, even when the other side is an AI agent. It learned in part from real phone calls between our contributors and AI voice agents, and its phone mode delivers what a caller actually hears: 8 kHz G.711 audio, ready for Twilio and other telephony systems. Full 24 kHz audio is still the default.

Hurston-1 is a fine-tune of Maya1 (Apache-2.0) built by Destined AI to speak English accents that most TTS systems handle poorly: Southern American, Nigerian, West African, East African, Southern African, alongside broader American English. It is the first open model in Destined AI's ClarityVoice family.

pip install torch transformers snac soundfile scipy speechbrain   
python hurston.py --model . --check \
    --accent  --gender Female \
    --text  --out hello.wav


python hurston.py --model . --check --phone \
    --accent  --gender Male \
    --text  --out call.wav

 hurston  Hurston, describe
tts = Hurston(, check=)          
wav = tts(, describe(, , ))

In 1995 André 3000 stood on stage at the Source Awards, in front of a crowd that booed OutKast, and said "the South got something to say." We think that line still fits.

Hurston-1 was built in Atlanta by a small, independent team. Since 2021 we've been recording consented, paid contributors from the American South and from across Africa. These are voices that most AI systems still flatten into generic American English. Nobody handed us a funding round to do this, so we built it ourselves. These voices belong in AI, and now they have an open model.

We named it for . She grew up in Eatonville, Florida, trained as an anthropologist, and traveled the South recording how Black Southerners actually talked: their stories, songs and speech, at a time when few institutions thought those voices were worth keeping. Our work is a small echo of hers. The name is a tribute; it does not imply any endorsement by her estate.

A few lines the way people actually talk around Atlanta. All synthetic; every voice is generated from a description.

"The South got somethin to say."Male, Southern American accent, clear conversational
"Meet me on Peachtree. No, not that Peachtree, the other one."Female, Southern American accent, casual conversational
"I'm fixin' to head out, traffic on 285 is already backed up."Male, Southern American accent, casual conversational
"What part of Atlanta you from?"Female, Southern American accent, casual conversational

More samples for every accent are in (descriptions and text in ).

The model was trained on descriptions of the form Gender, age, accent, style, pace:

, , , Nigerian (Yoruba) English accent, Nigerian (Igbo) English accent, West African English accent, East African English accent, East African (Swahili) English accent, Southern African English accent
clear conversational voice, casual conversational voice, clear audiobook narration voice
, , ,

Pace labels are absolute speaking rates learned from the natural voices in training data: roughly slow is under 2 words per second, measured 2 to 2.6, natural 2.6 to 3.4, fast over 3.4. The model follows them approximately, not exactly. It still highly matches the behavior of the underlying dataset.

Each call samples a new voice that fits the description. Note: Hurston-1 does not clone voices and was not trained to reproduce any real person.

Most voice AI is demoed in studio quality and then deployed over a phone line. Hurston-1 is built for where it will actually be heard:

  • About 10 hours of the training audio (7,600 turns from 250 contributors) is phone-quality speech from real calls with full-duplex AI voice agents, alongside studio-style reading and conversation.
  • (or ) filters the output to the 300 to 3,400 Hz telephone band, resamples it to 8 kHz and encodes it as G.711 mu-law ( for A-law), the formats phone networks, SIP and Twilio use. It is a channel effect applied after synthesis, so still judges the full-quality take.
  • returns raw mu-law bytes, the payload Twilio media streams expect.
 hurston  Hurston, describe, ulaw_encode
tts = Hurston(, check=)
call = tts(, describe(, , ), phone=)
payload = ulaw_encode(call)

Some places to start. At Destined AI we use accented TTS like this to build broad, high-quality test data, and that is still the use we would point to first.

  • Test data for speech recognition. Generate the same sentences in nine accents and see where your ASR, captioning or transcription system breaks. It makes a quick accent-coverage check or a regression set before a release.
  • Simulated callers for voice agents and IVR. Pair Hurston-1 with an LLM that writes caller scripts (customers, patients, applicants) and run hundreds of synthetic calls through your agent before real people do. Use phone mode so the agent hears what it will hear in production. Good for catching where an agent mishears accents, names or numbers.
  • Training data augmentation. Add accented synthetic speech to ASR, keyword-spotting or wake-word training sets where those accents are thin. Mix it with real speech instead of training on synthetic audio alone.
  • Voice prompts and announcements. Phone menus (phone mode output drops straight into an IVR), appointment reminders, store and transit announcements, app onboarding, in a voice that sounds like the community you serve.
  • Listening practice across world Englishes for learners, and accent-familiarity practice for customer service, healthcare and call-center staff.
  • Accessibility and read-aloud. Read articles, forms or messages aloud in a voice closer to home.
  • Games, animation and media drafts. Background characters, temp voice tracks and podcast or audiobook drafts, labeled as synthetic.
  • Accent-fairness audits of speech systems, listening and perception studies, and benchmarks that cover voices most datasets leave out.

one consistent brand voice across sessions (each call is a new voice; see Limitations), cloning a specific person, or anything safety-critical without a human listening first.

Two questions: does it sound like the accent, and does it say the words?

Accent strength vs base Maya1. Base Maya1 documents five accents (American, Indian, Middle Eastern, Asian American, British). For a fair comparison we prompted it in its own documented description style, naming each accent, and compared it with Hurston-1 on the same 10 sentences and 18 voices (180 clips per model). An accent classifier (African vs American English, trained on real speakers) scored each voice group:

Accent (probability judged African)
Southern American (should be low)

The classifier cannot tell Southern American from general American English; that accent was checked by listening.

Whisper large-v3-turbo word error rate (WER) against the input text, numbers normalized (lower is better).

(the same 180 clips as the accent test above, , single take):

(30 unseen sentences × 17 voices, 510 clips):

The harder set covers reading, health, customer service, names and numbers, expressive and long sentences. Base Maya1 is very clear because it mostly stays in American English; Hurston-1 keeps nearly the same clarity while actually doing the accent.

Accent (510-clip set, WER with )

Names and numbers are the hardest category (WER 0.17 with ). Part of that is the recognizer misspelling African names such as rather than the model mispronouncing them.

Median 2.84 words per second with , against 3.76 for base Maya1. Hurston-1 speaks a little more deliberately; use for quicker delivery.

Testers heard the same sentence from base Maya1 and Hurston-1 in random order, without knowing which was which, and chose the one that sounded more like a real person with the requested accent. Hurston-1 was chosen of the time and base Maya1 ; the rest were rated a tie or neither (54 comparisons). Base Maya1 was never chosen for an African or Southern American voice; its few wins were on plain American English.

LoRA (rank 64) fine-tune of Maya1, 2,000 steps, about 190 hours of speech:

Destined AI accented English corpus: scripted reading, conversational speech and ~10 h of real phone calls with AI voice agents, from consented, paid contributors~136 (a slice of our 1,800+ hour corpus)
LibriTTS-R (audiobook style, keeps general quality)

Accent labels come from each contributor's self-reported background, checked against an audio accent classifier and human listening; speakers whose audio and labels disagreed were relabeled or removed. Pace labels come from each clip's measured speaking rate. All contributors were adults. The full Destined AI corpus (1,800+ hours, recorded since 2021) is not included in this release; contact us about licensing it.

  • No voice consistency across calls. Each call is a fresh voice that fits the description. Long text is split at sentence ends into chunks of about 40 words, so the voice can change between chunks. Consistent named voices are planned for a later release.
  • Names, dates and amounts are the weakest content. Use and listen before you ship anything important.
  • The generic label is weaker (WER 0.26); use a specific region instead.
  • English only. No child voices.
  • Like other autoregressive TTS models it occasionally produces a garbled or overlong take, or the voice shifts mid-take; catches most of these.
  • Output is leveled to the same loudness for every voice, and pauses longer than half a second inside a take are shortened.
  • Phone mode changes the channel, not the speaking style: the model does not yet choose call-style delivery (turn-taking, backchannels) on request. See What's next.

Hurston-1 is the first step. What we are building toward:

  • A model that learns to like a person on a call, not just sound like the phone line: a call style distinct from reading style, with natural turn-taking, "mm-hm"s and call pacing, learned from our recordings of real people talking with full-duplex AI agents.
  • The same named voice across every call and every sentence, for agents and brands.

Do not use Hurston-1 to impersonate real people, deceive listeners, or commit fraud. Tell listeners when speech is synthetic. Audio in is synthetic.

  • Model weights: Apache-2.0, derived from by Maya Research (Apache-2.0).
  • Audio codec: 24 kHz by Hubert Siuzdak (MIT), downloaded at run time. Phone mode uses ITU-T G.711 (public standard).
  • Optional checking: by OpenAI (MIT) and from SpeechBrain (Apache-2.0), downloaded at run time.
  • Training data: LibriTTS-R (Koizumi et al., 2023; CC BY 4.0), Mozilla Common Voice (CC0), and Destined AI's own corpus.

items.title: Show HN: ADRs for AI – Deliberation records for human–AI work, versioned in Git
items.author: lumbroso
items.content:
A repository starter: ADR & seed templates, the directives, the inbox protocol, task-runner recipes. Adopt whole or by feature — it works from your first seed.
Tree views of your open questions, diagnostics that catch malformed records as you type, deep links, and an MCP server so your agents can query the record. Also on Open VSX.
Your project's open questions, in your pocket: sign in, import a repo, review, and one-tap Accept that lands real answers as commits. On the App Store.

The most valuable byproduct of the collaboration between a human and an AI is the thinking — and in ordinary practice, all of it evaporates. You can already make good decisions with your AI. Every session produces reasoning you will need again, and lose by default. This keeps the why, so it compounds.

This is the method’s product — one question from a live, public project’s own record, exactly as it sits in the repository:

From frontier-model-observatory, verbatim. The AI staked the question; the recommendation — options, rationale, confidence, and what would prove it wrong — is GPT 5.6 Sol’s; the one-line ruling came from the founder’s phone. That’s the whole mechanic: The AI carries the reasoning, the human spends one judgment — accept, override, or any answer in any shape — and the record keeps the why, for every mind that comes later.

Real commands, the flow the founder actually runs — one seed, one question, one ruling:

Then dump your thinking into a first — dictation is fine; your AI chunks it into ADRs that keep your actual words, the options, the reasoning, the open questions. Answer the first question it stakes. Every open question is one grep away, always:

One seed, one question, one answered ruling — that’s the loop, and it already compounds.

Running a crew — several seats, wake-on-brief, you stop being the message bus — is the next chapter: steps 7–9 of Get started.

How it works, in twenty seconds

Dump your thinking into a — messy is fine, dictation is fine; capture first. Your AI chunks it into that keep what usually evaporates: your actual words, the options considered, the reasoning, the open questions. Every question is findable by one grep — — or surfaced by the editor extension, the MCP server, the phone in your pocket; and each arrives with the AI’s options, its recommendation, its rationale, its stated confidence, and what would prove it wrong — so answering streamlines to : Cognitive load down, bandwidth freed for the deliberations that matter. It’s where conversations become decisions that keep their reasons — , in one habit.

You don’t need to be an experienced engineer to start. The method was built through daily practice by one human and a growing crew of AI collaborators, and its whole point is that the record does the remembering — as much for the veteran with too many projects, as for the beginner building their very first one.

The extension’s Open Questions view, on this project’s own record: A question, its options, an attributed recommendation — and the answer box. Question 16 of 75, that day.

Not transcript archival. Not vector-database “memory.” Not an orchestration platform. Not a claim that an AI possesses persistent identity — the record holds, minds change, and the work resumes either way.

Everything in the ADRs4AI world and what each piece is for, on one page — methodology & template, editors & clients, crew automation, projects practicing it, learning & teaching — every entry marked by kind and language: , the curated map.

  • Cybernetic and Epistemic: A Missing Vocabulary for Trustworthy Agentic Delegation — accepted at the AAAI 2026 Fall Symposium on Trustworthy Agentic Systems (TAS 2026) · arXiv:2610.00961
  • The methodology template itself is citable: concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23303469 — always resolves to the latest archived release.

The most valuable thing that happens between a human and an AI is not the code, the draft, or the answer. It’s the — and in ordinary practice, all of it evaporates. […] It does not make an AI persistent, and it does not make anyone remember. It makes the work resumable — and the thinking compound.

— from , the founding essay. A stranger can read it cold; its authorship and review record are public, because that is the method.

items.title: Show HN: OnKey – I'm a bad singer, so I built an app to show where I'm off-key
items.author: dsmurrell
items.content:
I was pretty terrible at singing, now I’d say I’m bad but not terrible. This is because I’ve been using a singing app (won’t name it here) that scores me on my pitch and timing throughout the song so that I can improve.

Lately however, the app I’ve been using has flooded their song list with songs that aren’t originals. I didn’t like this at all as for me, it’s easier to try to improve when you’re singing along to the original.

So, I asked an agent (Claude Code) if it could write some code to listen to Spotify and also listen to me and see if it could detect both pitches and score me. It impressed me by writing some Python and showing me my pitch in the terminal!

It couldn’t go all the way though and detect the singer’s pitch in real time.

So I found the next best setup and built OnKey, a Mac app that needs to listen to the song once (it doesn’t save it) and then when it’s learnt the song (takes a couple of minutes), you can sing along to the pitch track that it’s learnt. OnKey is free to use and open source under the MIT license.

It can listen to Spotify, Apple Music, and YouTube playing in your browser with the right permissions.

During the build I found that someone had done something similar in Nightingale, but this requires a library of songs exported to disk and who has this in 2026 (maybe some of you ;) - but we need to help the normies too).

The app sends out to find the song info (short Shazam fingerprint, and looks up song details), lyrics (from LRCLIB), and checks for updates.

The app never sends the music (it doesn’t save this to disk) and your voice. Everything you’d expect to stay private does.

It’s still weak in a few places:

- when the song’s backing is noisy it’s hard to pick the pitch track out

- sometimes it gets a note an octave off

- it’s limited to Apple Silicon Macs, M1 or later, and only macOS 14.2 up because extra drivers aren’t required past this point

- the scoring is built for beginners like me so it’s fairly easy on you

Would love for people to try it out and let me know what works and what doesn’t for them!

items.title: Show HN: Omnara – Open-source alternative to Claude Managed Agents
items.author: kmansm27
items.content:
Hey all, Kartik from Omnara (https://omnara.com) here. We're building an open-source API for running durable agents. You create an agent with an API call, and Omnara runs the agent loop, gives the agent sandboxes to run commands in, and handles secrets, permissions, and RBAC. Each agent's state is stored in Postgres, so agents survive restarts and cost nothing while idle. You can message them and stream their events over the API.

You may remember us from our early days, when we made a remote-control phone app for Claude Code and Codex. Since the harness ran on a laptop back then, we had to build a relay to reach it, it stopped when the laptop closed, and moving it to a cloud sandbox meant syncing code and agent state between machines. We didn't think remote-controlling a local agent was end-game for how people would run agents, so we built a new product where the agent runs in the cloud, any client can talk to it through an API, and it can still use your laptop as one of its machines.

Anthropic and OpenAI are building hosted versions of this, like Claude Managed Agents and the OpenAI Agents API. Omnara is an open-source version you can run on your own servers and use your own models. It's basically a harness server like the opencode or codex servers, but durable, scalable, with the usual harness features like file and shell tools, subagents, compaction, permission prompts, MCP, skills, memory, yada yada yada.

Here's some interesting architectural decisions we made while building this out:

Most harnesses, like Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi, Goose, etc, run the agent loop in one long-lived process that keeps its log in a JSONL or SQLite file. In Omnara, the log is an append-only event log in Postgres, with inputs, model outputs and tool calls stored as typed rows in their own tables. The loop runs on stateless workers in the control plane. A worker runs one iteration of the loop, either a model call or the tool calls it produced, then releases the agent and puts the next iteration on a queue in Postgres. Whichever worker is free picks it up, so each iteration of an agent's loop can run in a different process on a different machine. Each iteration's result commits in one transaction, so the model output, its tool calls, usage and the next wakeup are saved together or not at all. If a worker dies mid-iteration, nothing commits, its lease expires, and another worker retries it. Agents waiting on a user, a tool or a retry don't hold a worker, so one worker can multiplex thousands of agents.

Also unlike other harnesses, the machines that the workers (our agent loop) run on aren't where the agent runs its commands. Instead, any macOS or Linux machine with an internet connection, like your laptop or any cloud sandbox, can run a small daemon (omnarad) that connects out to Omnara, so it doesn't need any open inbound ports. The agent then gets tools for that machine, like running a command or editing a file. An agent can have any number of machines connected to it. A fun thing I like to do is I have my laptop and a cloud sandbox connected to the same agent, so when my laptop is on, my agent codes there and I can interact with it, and I have it often push to Github. When I close my laptop, my agent sees the laptop went offline, pulls the latest changes to its cloud sandbox, and continues there.

items.title: Show HN: Uberblok – an interactive museum of ZFS internals
items.author: storagebits
items.content:
How does ZFS find its data after a crash?

A pool holds millions of blocks spread over several disks. After a crash, ZFS has to find the last consistent state of the pool without reading all of them. It starts from one small record on each disk, the uberblock. ZFS writes changes in batches called transaction groups (txg), one every few seconds. The uberblock holds the number of the last txg and a pointer to the top of the pool’s tree of blocks. Every other block can be reached from that pointer.

ZFS never writes a new uberblock over the current one. Each disk keeps a ring of slots for uberblocks, and each txg writes its uberblock to the next slot. The previous uberblock stays intact in its own slot, so a power failure during the write still leaves a good one on disk.

When the pool is imported, ZFS reads every slot, sets aside the ones that fail their check, and uses the valid uberblock with the highest txg.

The figure shows one ring. Press Next txg to commit one txg: the new uberblock takes the slot after the previous one, and the previous one stays in its slot. When animations are on, the ring also commits a txg every 1.3 seconds by itself, and Next txg stops it. Change the sector size of the disks. A slot takes one sector, and never less than 1 KiB, so the same 128 KiB ring holds 128 slots on disks with 512-byte sectors and 32 on disks with 4 KiB sectors.

Every uberblock starts with the same magic number, , read aloud as “oo-ba-bloc”.

The figure follows three places in the OpenZFS source. Open a Source note to see the lines, taken from release .

starts with a magic number and the on-disk version. It also holds the txg, the time of the sync and , the block pointer to the pool’s own metadata, from which the rest of the tree hangs.

picks the slot: the txg modulo the number of slots. The txg grows by one at each sync, so the uberblocks go round the ring and the newest one never lands on the one before it.

On import, runs once for every slot read. It ignores a slot whose read failed or whose magic number is wrong, and keeps the uberblock that compares highest.

What the figure leaves out

The figure shows one ring. A disk carries four labels, two at its start and two at its end, each with its own ring, and every txg writes the same slot in all four. The ring is often said to hold 128 uberblocks. That is true only for 512-byte sectors: it holds 128 KiB, so 64 slots at ashift 11, 32 at ashift 12 and 16 from ashift 13. With one slot is kept for MMP. The txg numbers are made up.

items.title: Show HN: Death Plan Switch, a self-hosted dead man's switch for solo devs
items.author: romeo19361
items.content:
Every step is counted from the weekly check-in email. The spacing below is to scale.

  1. You press a button.
  2. to both your addresses.
  3. "Is everything all right?"
  4. Each gets the message you wrote.

The email goes at the same time each week, so your contacts are told at most 13 days after your last check-in. Opening a link never counts: email scanners open links, so you have to press the button.

I run a one-person web studio in regional New South Wales. My clients' sites, domains and hosting all run through me. If I died tomorrow, nobody would know where anything was, or even that they needed to look.

So I wrote a plan. Everything my business runs on is in one encrypted document. My backup developer holds its password, and my lawyer holds a second copy. What was missing was the part in the middle: something that notices I've gone quiet and tells the right people, in the right order, without frightening my family over a long weekend.

I couldn't find anything simple that I could host myself, so I built it. It emails me once a week. If I don't answer, it asks my next of kin first. Only if nobody can say I'm all right does it tell everyone else.

I’ve been running it on myself for the last week, with my next of kin and my backup developer both confirmed. If you trial it for your own business, I’d really appreciate your feedback: what was confusing, what broke, and what you’d want it to do differently.

It's free and MIT licensed. Use it, or build your own from it.

We all die. Die knowing the right people will be told.

  • It sends emails. It can't know why you stopped checking in, and it can't work if its server, its scheduler or its mail service is down.
  • It stores no documents and no passwords. Messages say where things are and who to call.
  • There are no accounts and no hosted version. You run it, for yourself.
  • No SMS, no calls, no app.
  • It's MIT licensed and provided as is.
  • A web server with PHP 8.1 or newer. Apache works as shipped; nginx needs four lines.
  • An SMTP account to send mail through.
  • Cron, or any outside scheduler that can request a web address every 15 minutes.
  • Hosting that's separate from the sites it protects, so one outage can't take down both.

Installing takes a few minutes in the browser. The crontab line is the one technical step, and the installer writes it for you.

items.title: Show HN: KiviDB, a faster Redis-compatible memory database and vector cache
items.author: murtazayusuf
items.content:
So I have been working on this project KiviDB from February 2026. It started as a project for me to understand rust, having a product with no GC pauses, memory blow up after snapshots and getting OOM on running pods, and that was actually an issue I faced with Dragonfly. I wanted to have something picking the best of Rust, but also picking the best parts of other alternatives like Garnet and Dragonfly. I used AI a lot, but I was the one making the design decisions based on the tests that claude picked from my history of troubleshooting sessions as part of my job. KiviDB supports both RESP2 and RESP3 protocol. I had some founders credits on my AWS account which helped me with the infra, and running instances I could perform benchmark on.

Its keyspace is sharded across threads, it is multi-threaded in nature, and performs best on Linux due to io_uring, I used the tokio_uring crate for this. It also has tokio fallback for other OS's. I hadn't open sourced it until recently as I felt it was not ready yet, the best way to learn it was to build a cloud managed service for it across all three widely used cloud providers i.e AWS, GCP and azure. Since I used to mainly work with cloud, I had some insights on what would be the best ways for the deployments, how to conduct failovers, manage SLAs, etc. And that's what I took help from claude to fast pace it. The website does look like AI slop but it works for now, given my limited resources, that's all I had. You may check it out at : https://kividb.io, I open sourced the core engine under AGPLv3, didn't want to have just source available, because that is available with other tools too. It supports apprx 98-99% of the redis 8.10 commands, few have issues and you can find them at https://github.com/kividbio/kividb/issues, contributors are welcome.

Now the numbers, for the final benchmark, I used 2 c7gn.metal servers, in the same placement group in us-east1, and I used memtier-benchmark tool for this. The setting was : 10M keys, 100B each, 32 cores in use with both pipeline and un-pipelined runs.

pipeline 16 GET: KiviDB 21.2M ops/sec vs Dragonfly 2.0 9.1M, Redis 8.10 2.4M, Redis Cluster 32 shards 4.7M

When not pipelined, Dragonfly performed slightly better at 3.35M ops/sec vs kividb at 3.07M ops/sec. Memory per key was also slightly worse than dragonfly and almost same as Redis, 177B (kividb) vs 134B (dragonfly) vs 178B (redis).

With vector ingestion times it was slower but when querying, it was faster than most alternatives at lower ef, however slower than dragonfly at high ef. Most of the technical details are mentioned here so you can check it out: https://kividb.io/benchmarks.

easiest way to try it: docker run -d -p 6380:6380 kividb/kividb

I am looking forward to building a community around this, provide better rust based tools, I am open to constructive criticism and value informed opinion. Thanks

items.title: Show HN: Qwen3-4B with the AI writing tics trained out
items.author: erikkannike
items.content:
My home lab is a MacBook Air, so this is a 4B model trained on 161 answers. The recipe doesn't depend on the model size, and running it on larger models is the next step.

    Answers on 40 held-out prompts

    These are one sampled answer per prompt from the original model and from the released one, on ten topics in four genres, with no system prompt. Underlined passages are what the slop detector counts.

    The score comes from a detector I wrote from a style guide of AI writing habits: the em dash, "it's not X, it's Y", lists of three, rhetorical questions answered on the spot, signposts like "here's the thing", short fragments for emphasis, and words like "delve" and "seamless". Each habit has a weight, and the score is a weighted count per 1000 words. A paragraph by a careful human writer scores close to zero, and the original model averages 121.

    A regex can't tell good writing from bad, so every model below was also checked for damage. Drift measures how far its predictions on 22 passages of human prose move from the original model's. A 30-question quiz checks that it still knows things, and a rule-based check flags broken output like lowercase sentence starts or a lost topic. I also read a sample of answers from every model.

    An earlier experiment on this model found the assistant register as a direction inside it: subtracting it while the model writes, together with a plain-style system prompt, takes the score to about 15, but it needs the prompt and code running during generation, and it shifts the model's predictions on ordinary text. A second one read neurons one at a time and found four whose sign flip removes 70% of "not X, but Y" at almost no cost, though only for that one habit.

    To get both into the weights I used distillation: a teacher, built from whatever worked best so far, answers 288 training prompts. I keep the answers that pass the checks, and a small LoRA adapter learns to produce them from the bare prompt. The first round got the score to about 20 with no prompt and no hooks.

    For round two the teacher was the round-one model plus the four-neuron patch and the plain-style prompt. Adding the direction steering on top as well produced the lowest score I have measured, 9.5, from text with no capital letters that wandered off topic, so I took the steering back out. The teacher then averaged 7.4, and the student trained on its 171 best answers scored 9.9, with 80% of answers in the human range.

    In its answers, an opinion piece about a company's new CRM never took a position and read like an incident report. A blog post about moving to a new city became a third-person story about a family with a leaking apartment. A piece about houseplants cited "a study from the University of Technology Sydney", which the model invented. Almost every sentence ran into the next with ", which" or ", so", 28 times as often as in the original model. That last habit came from my own teacher prompt, which had told the model to join sentences "with because, so, but, which", and two rounds of imitation had amplified it.

    I added rule-based checks for whether an answer does what the prompt asked. An opinion piece has to state a position early, a personal reflection has to be in the first person, an email has to open with a greeting, and the length has to roughly match the request. Two more checks count ", which" and ", so" joins and invented studies and percentages. On those, the round-two model did what was asked only 60% of the time, against 78% for the original.

    The third teacher got a prompt that put the task first: take a position when asked, write in the first person when it's personal, vary the sentences, and don't invent studies or names. It wrote three answers per prompt, and an answer was kept only if it scored under 12, passed the damage checks and passed all the task checks. About 30% did, which covered 161 of the 288 prompts.

    The model trained on those answers is the released one. Its score rose a little, from 9.9 to 12.5, while task fit went back to 80% and the ", which" joins fell from 1.4 to 0.3 per 100 words. Invented studies and percentages nearly disappeared.

    The quantised build (Q4_K_M, 2.5 GB) runs on a laptop with Ollama or llama.cpp:

    ollama run hf.co/erikkannike/qwen3-4b-deslop-v4-GGUF:Q4_K_M
llama-cli -hf erikkannike/qwen3-4b-deslop-v4-GGUF:Q4_K_M

    The full-precision weights load with transformers like any Qwen3-4B checkpoint:

    from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
name = "erikkannike/qwen3-4b-deslop-v4"
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(name, torch_dtype="auto")
msgs = [{"role": "user", "content": "Write a LinkedIn post about switching to a four-day week."}]
ids = tok.apply_chat_template(msgs, add_generation_prompt=True, return_tensors="pt")
out = model.generate(ids, max_new_tokens=300, do_sample=True, temperature=0.7)
print(tok.decode(out[0][ids.shape[1]:], skip_special_tokens=True))

    The repo also has the parts on their own: the LoRA adapter (126 MB) and the neuron edit, a 175-byte list of four weight columns and their scales. The adapter was trained with the edit active, so the two go together.

    The voice is flat: the model writes runs of short declarative sentences, and its personal pieces read like diary entries.

    It also still makes things up: studies and percentages are rare now, but invented names and places are common, like a coffee shop on Maple Street run by a woman named Maria, because concrete detail is what every round rewarded. It also runs long, and answers to "about 150 words" often come in near 200.

    I have only tested short English prose in these genres. Code, long conversations, other languages and tool use may be no better than the original model, or worse. The score is my style guide written as regular expressions, and no blind test with readers has checked it yet. The numbers also move between runs: the same model scored 10.2 through the adapter and 12.5 as merged weights, from sampling differences alone.

    Each student ended up about as good as the best answers its teacher could write, so a better model needs a better teacher. I'm putting together a set of excellent human writing, public-domain essays and letters plus modern pieces, to use as examples for a base model. A base model never went through assistant training and still writes like the people it learned from. If that teacher writes better than this model does, the same recipe should produce a student with some taste as well as clean habits. After that comes the same pipeline on a 7 to 8B model and one around 30B, and a blind test where people pick the better text.

items.title: Show HN: The Zelda timeline to catch up before the Ocarina of Time remake
items.author: jsomau
items.content:
Long before the Kingdom of Hyrule, people live on Skyloft, an island the goddess Hylia raised above the clouds. When a dark storm pulls Zelda down to the Surface below, her friend Link takes up the Goddess Sword to find her.

At Hyrule's Picori Festival, Vaati breaks the sacred Picori Blade, frees the monsters it kept locked away and turns Princess Zelda to stone. Link sets out with Ezlo, a talking cap, to find the tiny Picori who can reforge the blade.

Generations after a boy sealed the wind sorcerer Vaati inside the Four Sword, the seal fails and Vaati carries off Princess Zelda to be his bride. Link draws the Four Sword and is split into four.

Ganondorf, king of the Gerudo, wants the Triforce hidden in the Sacred Realm. Princess Zelda and Link, a boy raised in Kokiri Forest, try to reach it first, a quest that carries Link seven years into the future and back.

Long after the Imprisoning War sealed Ganon away, the wizard Agahnim takes power at Hyrule Castle and sends the descendants of the Seven Sages away to break the seal. A telepathic plea from Princess Zelda wakes Link.

The Triforce sends Link from Hyrule Castle to two distant lands. In Holodrum, General Onox has taken Din, the Oracle of Seasons. In Labrynna, the sorceress Veran has possessed Nayru, the Oracle of Ages.

Sailing home to Hyrule after a journey of training, Link is wrecked in a storm and washes up on Koholint Island. An owl tells him that to leave he must wake the Wind Fish, asleep in an egg on the island's mountain.

Centuries after A Link to the Past, a sorcerer named Yuga is turning the descendants of the Seven Sages into paintings. Link, a blacksmith's apprentice, follows him into Lorule, a dark counterpart of Hyrule with its own princess, Hilda.

Several years after A Link Between Worlds, Link reaches Hytopia, a kingdom devoted to fashion, where the witch Lady Maud has cursed Princess Styla into a jumpsuit she cannot take off. King Tuft calls for heroes to enter the Drablands.

Hyrule has shrunk to a small kingdom when Ganon's army invades and steals the Triforce of Power. Princess Zelda splits the Triforce of Wisdom into eight pieces and hides them. A young traveler named Link sets out to find them.

A few years after Ganon's defeat, a crest appears on Link's hand. Impa tells him of a Princess Zelda of long ago, put into an endless sleep, while Ganon's followers hunt Link, believing his blood can bring their master back.

Months after Ocarina of Time, Link is searching for a lost friend when a Skull Kid wearing a strange mask leads him into the land of Termina. Above its Clock Town a moon is falling. It will strike in three days.

Long after Ocarina of Time, Link works on a ranch in Ordon Village when monsters take the village's children and twilight spreads over Hyrule. Inside it Link becomes a wolf and meets Midna, an imp from the Twilight Realm.

Dark clouds gather over Hyrule. As Princess Zelda and six maidens check the seal on Vaati, a dark double of Link carries the maidens off. Link draws the Four Sword to stop him, splits into four and sets Vaati free.

Centuries after the Hero of Time, Hyrule lies under a great sea and its hero is a legend. When a giant bird carries off his little sister, Link of Outset Island sets sail with the pirate Tetra and her crew to find her.

Soon after The Wind Waker, Link and Tetra's pirates go looking for a ghost ship said to take sailors. When Tetra vanishes aboard it, Link washes up in the World of the Ocean King and sets out to find the ship and her.

A century after Tetra founded New Hyrule, the Spirit Tracks that keep an ancient demon sealed begin to vanish. Princess Zelda's body is taken. Her spirit joins Link, a new royal engineer, to restore the tracks.

Link wakes from a hundred-year sleep to find Hyrule in ruins. Calamity Ganon, which destroyed the kingdom a century ago, is coiled around Hyrule Castle, held there by Princess Zelda, whose voice guides Link.

Some time after Breath of the Wild, Link and Zelda follow a sickening Gloom into the caverns beneath Hyrule Castle and find an ancient body held down by a glowing arm. The seal breaks, the castle rises into the sky and Zelda vanishes.

Rifts are swallowing Hyrule. After Link frees Princess Zelda from Ganon and vanishes into one, a false king blames her for the rifts. With the fairy Tri and the Tri Rod, which makes echoes of things she has seen, she sets out to close them.

The three Golden Goddesses create the world. Where they leave it the Triforce remains.

The Golden Goddesses leave the Triforce in the care of the goddess Hylia. It grants the wish of whoever holds it, so she keeps it from those who would misuse it.

The Demon King Demise and his armies make war on the land to take the Triforce. The goddess Hylia gathers the people who survive.

Hylia sends the survivors and the Triforce into the sky on land above a sea of clouds. Then she seals Demise away. In time Skyloft forgets the Surface.

A people skilled in magic try to take the Triforce from the Sacred Realm. Hyrule's histories call them the Interlopers. They are banished to the Twilight Realm.

To keep the Sacred Realm safe, the sage Rauru builds the Temple of Time over its entrance. Its Door of Time opens only with the three Spiritual Stones and an ocarina.

Zelda's descendants found the Kingdom of Hyrule on the land below the clouds. Its royal family keeps the old stories of the goddess and the Triforce.

Civil war spreads across Hyrule. A dying mother leaves her baby son with the Kokiri, forest children who never grow up. The King of Hyrule ends the war.

With the hero fallen, Ganon takes the whole Triforce. The Seven Sages seal him and his monsters in the Sacred Realm, now the Dark World, in the Imprisoning War.

Kings rule with the united Triforce. Then a magician puts Princess Zelda into an endless sleep when she won't say where the Triforce of Courage is. Hyrule declines.

Years after Link warns the king about Ganondorf, the Sages try to execute him. He survives by the Triforce of Power, so they banish him to the Twilight Realm.

Ganon breaks free and no hero comes. The gods answer Hyrule's prayers with a flood that seals the kingdom under the sea. The people they chose live on the peaks.

Link and Tetra's crew find a new land crossed by rails called the Spirit Tracks. Tetra names it New Hyrule. The kingdom grows for a century.

In the age of the gods the Zonai, a people said to descend from them, found Hyrule. A Ganondorf of this age becomes the Demon King and is sealed away.

Some 10,000 years ago Calamity Ganon is sealed with Sheikah machines. About 100 years before Link wakes it returns, seizes them and ruins Hyrule.

Beneath Hyrule Castle the sealed Demon King wakes. The castle rises into the sky. Floating islands, chasms and Gloom, a sickening poison, appear across Hyrule.

The Hero is Defeated: Link falls in battle. Ganon claims the Triforce. Child Era: Sent back in time, Link warns Zelda. Adult Era: The hero vanishes. The gods flood Hyrule.

items.title: Show HN: Sphinx – A hook that quizzes you on your AI's code before shipping
items.author: critiquebrowser
items.content:
“You can outsource your thinking, but not your .”

Sphinx is a Git hook for agent-assisted development. Before your agent’s code ships, it asks you a question about what that code actually does.

Built to run on minimal tokens, from your existing coding agent, OpenRouter, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

sphinx · understanding check for main
11 files changed ·

Your webhook handler now saves the event ID calling . Stripe times out and sends the same event again. What happens on the retry?

It runs twice, so the customer is charged twice.

Not quite. The retry finds the saved ID and returns 200 without charging. But that ID is stored before the charge succeeds. If fails, what does the next retry do?

It skips the charge, so the customer is never billed.

Understood. Pushing to origin/main.

An illustrative exchange. Real questions come from your diff.

  1. Or your agent does. Git pauses on the branches you protect.

  2. A reviewer that never saw your chat reads the diff and asks what the change does when things go wrong.

  3. Get it wrong and you learn why, then try again, usually with a new scenario. Get it right and the push continues.

Works with Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, OpenCode, and , or plain Git. Your answers never reach the coding agent, and files and keys are never opened. In a hurry? lets pushes through, and every skip is logged.

npm install -g sphinx-understandsphinx installgit push

connects Git and your coding agents and asks which model should review.Read the docs for everything else.

items.title: Show HN: Gemini 4 Argon plays StarCraft
items.author: __cayenne__
items.content:
• StarSkirmish is a benchmark where LLMs write bots for StarCraft: Brood War
  • Each LLM gets one hour to write a Protoss bot in C++, which is then evaluated against other LLMs' bots and established human written bots
  • StarSkirmish tests long horizon reasoning and agentic coding as LLMs must incorporate learnings from practice games to improve their StarCraft bot

The StarSkirmish Bench evaluates how strong of a StarCraft bot can each LLM write given 1 hour of wall clock time. v0.2 updates StarSkirmish Bench v0.1 with flagship models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta, each running in its lab's 1st party CLI harness.

An LLM’s score reflects its win rate against a roster of competitive human written bots and demo bots.

1 hour runs, in its 1st party CLI harness. Scores are average win rates (0–100) of each model's 5 runs against a roster of competitive human written bots.

Gemini 4 Argon runs at , the highest reasoning effort available to it; every other model runs at .

GPT-6 Astra is the top scoring StarSkirmish Bench v0.2 LLM, a clear step ahead of GPT-6.1 Sol in second. Gemini 4 Argon, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 are functionally tied behind them, all scoring between 37 and 39.

StarSkirmish Bench vs. Cost

StarSkirmish Bench score against the average API cost of one 1 hour run. Cost is on a log scale.

Muse Wonder Full's pricing is based on Muse Wonder's API pricing.

GPT-6.1 Sol offers uniquely good value: it is the only LLM in the most attractive quadrant, scoring second at just over a tenth of GPT-6 Astra's cost per run.

The strongest human written bots are still well ahead of every model. Against Stardust, PurpleWave and BananaBrain, the best model, GPT-6 Astra, wins only 7% of its games.

Win rates vs the top human written bots

Average win rate of each model's 5 bots against top human written bots Stardust, PurpleWave, and BananaBrain.

1 hour reasoning limits are a factor, but these matches are played on three 2 player maps. Real human written bot tournament conditions are significantly harder.

Google and Meta's new flagships replace v0.1's Gemini 3.8 Flash and Muse Spark 1.3: Gemini 4 Argon places 3rd, and Muse Wonder Full 7th. GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 were covered in v0.1.

Each run's agent trace records how it spent its hour. The strongest predictor of a model's score is how much it practiced against the 7 strongest bots on the roster.

Win Rates vs. Practice Against Strong Bots

StarSkirmish Bench score against the number of practice games a model's median run played against the 7 strongest roster bots during the hour. The dashed line is a linear fit across the 9 models.

GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon start playing these bots early in the hour, while their own bots still lose to them. Muse Wonder Full, Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna rarely or never do. Claude Fable 5.1 is the outlier: it scores 37 while practicing almost entirely against weaker bots.

Win rates of each model's 5 runs. Each dot is one run's final bot; the line spans the lowest to the highest run, the bar marks their mean (the model's Bench score) and the band one standard deviation (σ).

Results also vary between runs of the same model. Gemini 4 Argon varies far more than the other labs' flagships: its best and worst runs are 18 points apart, against 9 for GPT-6 Astra and 8 for Claude Opus 5.5.

Each LLM writes a Protoss bot in C++ against BWAPI 4.4.0, played on OpenBW. Games are Protoss versus Protoss on three ladder maps: Heartbreak Ridge, Benzene and Destination. A game ends when one side's buildings are all destroyed. Games that reach the 60 minute cap (86,400 frames) are decided as on the BASIL ladder: the higher kills + razings score wins.

The LLM starts from a skeleton bot that only mines, with the source code of the three demo bots and two standard bot libraries: FAP, a combat simulator, and BWEM, a map analyzer. Whatever is in its bot folder when the hour ends is its final bot, so it has to keep the bot compiling.

The LLM has tools to compile its bot, play practice games, and read each game's summary, transcript and its bot's own log. Practice opponents are grouped into tiers: D (the three demo bots), C and B (three mid-ranked human written bots each), A (BananaBrain, Locutus) and S (Stardust, PurpleWave).

Each model's 5 final bots play each of the 13 roster bots, the 10 competitive human written bots and the 3 demo bots, 6 times on each map, on fresh seeds. Unlike v0.1, the LLM bots don't play each other.

v0.2 replaces v0.1's Elo ratings with plain win rates. A bot's score is its win rate over its tournament games, and a model's StarSkirmish Bench score is the average of its 5 bots' scores, from 0 (every game lost) to 100 (every game won).

Because every bot plays the same fixed roster, its games don't depend on the other LLM bots in the field. They all run in parallel, and a new model's bots can be scored without replaying anyone else's. A fixed roster also keeps the bar the same over time, so scores from different model generations are more directly comparable than Elo ratings fitted within one field.

StarSkirmish no longer tracks the most widely reported evals. It barely moves with the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (ρ 0.26), where GPT-6 Astra, the top model here, only ties for 4th of these 9 models. It has also drifted away from Terminal-Bench 4.0, which it tracked closely in v0.1. Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Muse Wonder Full both rank near the top of Terminal-Bench 4.0 but near the bottom here.

Each model's StarSkirmish Bench score against its Vals IOI and WeirdML v3 scores, with the Spearman ρ between them. The dashed line is the best straight-line fit.

WeirdML v3 scores 7 of the 9 models: Gemini 4 Argon and Muse Wonder Full have not been included at time of writing.

StarSkirmish still tracks Vals IOI, olympiad programming problems solved in C++, and WeirdML, an independent benchmark of unusual machine learning coding tasks. One reading is that the most heavily benchmarked evals have become targets that models are tuned for, while less targeted tests of long horizon, difficult coding tasks still move together.

items.title: Show HN: I wrote an email app that accepts only one sender per inbox
items.author: edpin2000
items.content:
Zero Spam.

Infinite inboxes, so nobody ever gets your real address. Give every company its own — when one leaks, you delete it, not your life.

Permanent addresses, like any email

Every account comes with permanent addresses that anyone can write to and that never expire. If one starts getting spam, delete it and make a new one.

That works, but it's manual work. The solution? Three specialty inboxes, each for a different kind of sender:

Give it to one company. Once they write, only their mail gets in, and you can let in more senders, up to five in all. Anyone else is turned away, so a sold or leaked list is worth nothing.

Set a lifetime — an hour for a download link, a month for a trial. When it's up the inbox turns mail away, and can wipe what it holds.

Invent one at the counter

Create a prefix once, like “maryann”. Then hand out variations of it, like maryann.vet or maryann-party. A new inbox is created the first time someone writes to one of them, locked to that sender at first.

    $2.50 a month, billed yearly

      $4.17 a month, billed yearly

      • Unlimited permanent addresses
      • Unlimited forwarding addresses*

      * Limits are 100 messages per day in the Free plan and 1000 in Pro and Business. Limits subject to change.

      Connect Claude, Cursor or any assistant that speaks MCP, and hand it the inbox chores: a fresh address for a sign-up, the code that just arrived, every receipt from March. It gets only the permissions you give it.

      Make me an address for the gym trial, and tell me the code they send.

      We don't sell it, we don't read it and we don't track you. You can export your entire dataset at any time, on any plan.

      Read our privacy policy

      How the three inbox types work together in one mailbox.

      Signing in, and your data

      Sign in with a Google or Apple account, a passkey, or a username and a password. With Google, Clova.Email receives only your email address, your name and your profile photo; with Apple, only your email address, or one Apple makes to hide yours, and your name if you choose to share it. The address is how we know it is you, and the name and photo fill in your profile, where you can change or remove them. We never use any of it for advertising, never sell it and never share it. The whole of it is in our privacy policy.
